title: My Apology to American Democracy
text:
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. 

 A fter any election, it’s natural to hunt for results that prove you were right all along. Landslides in particular provide the winners with ample evidence to sustain just about every prior position. At the moment, Democrats are engaged in a familiar argument over which faction, the progressives or the moderates, can claim responsibility for the party’s remarkable new majority. If you support Medicare for All, you’ll point to Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan. If you’re a skeptic, Roy Cooper of North Carolina won the election’s biggest blowout for a flipped Senate seat. If you want to retire the culture war, look at Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico in Texas. If you thought the race was about Palestine and trans issues, Victoria Broderick just became Tennessee’s first queer member-elect of Congress. Latinos, independents, southern Black women, men under 30, the white working class: bragging rights for all.

 But it might be more useful to search for what you got wrong. Views that are exploded by subsequent events have a way of disappearing from the mind, making it easy to forget you ever held them in the first place, and creating an illusion that your political wishes always accord with reality. We’re all prone to squeezing facts into the shape of narratives we carry in our heads and ignoring facts that undermine them. These mental habits contribute to a culture of total vindication and no compromise. They also make it difficult to understand present events or predict future ones.

 Last year, I wrote that America was becoming an authoritarian state. There were grounds for believing it. Think back to the country that America seemed to have become. President Trump ruled with almost no checks on his power. The Supreme Court offered little resistance and Congress none, as if the Constitution had been suspended and the entire federal government had come under the control of one man. The civil service had been gutted, independent agencies neutered, and the Justice Department warped into the president’s personal tool for rewarding friends, punishing enemies, and enriching himself. Long-standing norms of language, behavior, and probity collapsed daily. Elites in business, media, academia, and law lay supine before Trump’s demands for fealty and lucre. After returning to power a man who had tried to nullify democracy, the public seemed entirely passive: content, checked out, or too stunned to react.

 [ Listen: Autocracy in America ] 

 Remember the fear, the confusion turning to panic. Masked gunmen swept through American neighborhoods, foreigners stayed away from American airports, and international students began to disappear from American universities. After Charlie Kirk’s murder, the White House set out to purge his detractors, and Stephen Miller warned the enemies of goodness—perhaps half the country—that they had awakened a dragon. In red towns, regime critics lowered their voices. In blue cities, families talked seriously about the possibility of moving to another country. Famous figures in the resistance began to leave , while some people I knew tried to parlay a deceased grandparent into a foreign passport and had their children apply to overseas colleges. How could you raise kids here? What if the previous election had returned to power a president who would make sure there would never be another?

 No one wanted to be the fool who waited too long to get out. But how would you know when it was too late? Having no experience with these dilemmas, we looked to history for guidance. The spirit of the moment was captured in a recent translation of The Oppermanns , written in 1933 by the German Jewish novelist Lion Feuchtwanger, who had the foresight to flee as soon as Hitler came to power. The lesson seemed to be: Get out while you still can.

 In its annual democracy index for 2025, Freedom House gave the United States its lowest score ever—on par with South Africa and below Panama. Political minds debated what to call this radical deformation of democracy: right-wing populist, illiberal, authoritarian, patrimonialist—even fascist. I wrote an article about this ominous state of affairs with the title “ America’s Zombie Democracy .”

 Now a free election has delivered an overwhelming rebuke to Trump and his rule. What kind of fascist allows that to happen?

 I f I were to summarize the flaws in my own thinking, I would say that I overrated Trump’s competence as a dictator, and I underrated the resilience of American democracy. “I don’t think that people were wrong to be worried, and I don’t think the threat is over,” Lawrence Norden, an election-security expert at the Brennan Center for Justice, told me. “I do think maybe some people underestimated the ability to fight back.”

 Trump wants to rule as a fascist. His governing style emulates the classic features of fascism: cult of the leader, nationalist and xenophobic rhetoric, glorification of the “real” people, demonization of minorities and political opponents, relish for violence, a blizzard of propaganda and lies. Last January, at what was probably the peak of his power following the raid on Venezuela, he declared that only “my own morality, my own mind,” could stop him from doing anything he wanted around the world.

 But Trump is too shallow, undisciplined, and selfish to lead a great movement with an idealistic vision of the state that can outlive him. He has spent much of his second term distracted by vanity construction projects and self-enrichment schemes. His lifelong attraction to crassly beautiful women has become, in his less priapic ninth decade, an attraction to crassly rich men—Elon Musk, Larry Ellison, Jensen Huang. Trump, his family, and his circle have shown their contempt for the MAGA base by descending into unprecedented depths of corruption at a time of rising prices and interest rates. A competent dictator wouldn’t lose touch with the people whose voice he claims to be. He wouldn’t allow his regime to take the place of the arrogant elites who had served as foils on his way to power. He wouldn’t keep harping on his new ballroom. Trump is a failed fascist.

 Just as Americans who have known no system other than liberal democracy struggle to imagine its downfall, to understand an authoritarian American president, we tried to compare him to analogues past and present. When Trump was first elected, in 2016, a friend said, “We have to hope he’s Berlusconi, not Mussolini.” Trump is both, and the mix of showman and strongman makes him harder to predict than either one separately. It’s intellectually more straightforward to think of him in the mold of a figure like Vladimir Putin than, say, Alberto Fujimori. It’s also emotionally more satisfying: The lines are clear; the stakes couldn’t be higher; a great battle is on. When, a year ago, I wrote the words “We are living in an authoritarian state,” I felt a shudder of fear and gloom, but also, unmistakably, of excitement.

 I thought that in his second term Trump would focus single-mindedly on keeping and using power. In the first year he did, and many of us worried that in the second year he might rig or annul the midterms. This wasn’t a far-fetched concern: Trump tried to change voting rules, disqualify registered voters, intimidate election officials with threats of criminal charges, mobilize the Justice Department to challenge results. With election denialists holding key state offices and rogue immigration agents possibly guarding the polls, Trump could keep an irrevocably gerrymandered Congress Republican and harden MAGA’s lock on power. Then he might find a way to continue as president for a third term or install one of his children in the White House.

 None of this was a fever dream, but it gave Trump too much credit. As it turned out, the midterms held his attention only fitfully. When courts struck down his executive orders, he didn’t defy them. When people in Minneapolis found the courage to protest the thugs with guns who were terrorizing their neighbors and killing American citizens, Trump backed off. Almost on a whim, he started a ruinous war with Iran. While his popularity sank, he went about relining the Reflecting Pool, changing the interior design of the White House ballroom, and enlarging plans for the Triumphal Arch. He spent a lot of time organizing garish celebrations of America’s 250th birthday, claiming it as his own. Actually governing the country hardly seemed to interest him. His appearances in the fall campaign grew more and more bizarre—no one remembers anything from those speeches except a few obscene insults and a peculiar fixation on a Republican senator’s buttocks. Historical analogies pointed to the Roman emperor Caligula. And when, on November 3, the voters gave a shattering blow to Trump and his movement—a loss too big to rig or overturn—his initial response was a shrug. After all, his name wasn’t on the ballot. Within the gilded walls of his own mind, he remained undiminished.

 Whereas Trump proved unequal to the demands of holding autocratic power, American democracy in 2026 showed a resilience that seemed to have disappeared in 2025. A year ago I thought that little stood between Trump and the consolidation of authoritarian rule. The institutions were hollow and the elites spineless. But this year two of those institutions made sure that the public would have a say: the federal courts and the state and local election system. Almost every attempt by the administration to change voting rules, interfere with election officials, and manipulate the vote count was blocked by the courts, including, in at least one case, the Supreme Court. Election officials around the country resisted the administration’s efforts to intimidate them. Norden, of the Brennan Center, said, “We are lucky that we have a very decentralized election system in the U.S., and the states and civil society were able to take advantage of that to be ready for the assault.” So the people would get a chance to speak.

 [ Read: How Americans defeated an autocrat-in-waiting ] 

 Despite Trump’s abysmal ratings, I hadn’t forgotten that this electorate returned him to power after he had summoned a mob to try to stop the peaceful transition of power for the first time since the Civil War. Nothing has ever shaken my faith in my compatriots like a presidential election in which the price of eggs mattered more than the fate of democracy.

 The midterms showed that democracy still matters to most Americans—fitfully, like Trump’s interest in ruling, and not necessarily as a set of abstract concepts called separation of powers , rule of law , and independent judiciary , but in a more visceral way, as a sense of fairness and common decency. Few Americans cared about the destruction of foreign aid by a private citizen who happens to be the richest man in the world. The firing of inspectors general across the federal government aroused little protest. But this didn’t mean that the public had entirely lost its self-respect. Americans who voted for Trump three times were still capable of turning against him.

 Throughout the year, offense at Trump’s callous excesses slowly rose until it became unstoppable. His greatest mistake was thinking that his spectacular corruption would be of no concern to ordinary people, as if grift on a grand scale came with the divine right to rule. Americans are more likely to ignore abuses of power when times are good. But in a year when health premiums along with the price of gas and diesel spiked, Trump’s gold ballroom and Qatari jet affronted a people who apparently still believe that they are their own masters in a self-governing republic. They just had to be reminded.

 It was better to exaggerate than underrate Trump’s ability to bring 250 years of democracy to an end. For a distracted and amnesiac people, sleepwalking into authoritarianism remains a risk; the vigilance aroused by Trump’s lawless presidency should be our constant state. But those 250 years have left expectations and habits in American minds that, though they might disappear for a time, are not easily killed.
